01.event: Ulla praises Rav Hamnuna but casts doubt on his lineage because he is from Harpanya
01.turn: Rav Hamnuna is ashamed; Ulla asks where he pays his poll tax
01.outcome: Ulla concludes he belongs to Pum Nahara, so his lineage is not flawed
01.summary: Rav Hamnuna sat studying before Ulla, who praised him but lamented that he came from Harpanya, a town of flawed lineage. Rav Hamnuna was embarrassed. Ulla asked where he paid his poll tax, and on hearing Pum Nahara, declared him to be from Pum Nahara, clearing his lineage.
01.reason: Mainly dialogue, but there is conflict (a slur on lineage), an emotional reaction that counts as an event, and a change when the slur is withdrawn. Mainly speech with something happening fits R-C7 shape 1.

02.actor: residents of an alleyway; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
02.event: a case of an alleyway bounded by the sea and a garbage dump came before Rabbi
02.outcome: Rabbi said neither prohibited nor permitted; the Gemara explains why
02.summary: An alleyway bounded on one side by the sea and on the other by a garbage dump was brought before Rabbi, who gave no ruling either way. The Gemara then explains his silence.
02.missing: any action or change beyond the case being brought to the rabbi
02.reason: The only event is that the case came before a rabbi, who then did not rule; segment 3 is the Gemara's commentary. Under R-C0's limit this is not a story.

03.actor: a man in Mata Mehasya and his brother
03.event: a yevama falls to the man; his brother wants to disqualify her with a bill of divorce
03.turn: the man offers to share the estate; the brother fears being cheated like the Pumbedita swindler
03.outcome: the man offers to let him take his share at once
03.summary: A man became bound to his brother's widow in Mata Mehasya, and another brother wanted to disqualify her with a get. The man offered to split the property; the brother feared a swindle like the one in Pumbedita, so the man offered to divide it immediately.
03.missing: what actually happened afterwards; the passage is a negotiation that ends in an offer
03.reason: There is a real situation (the levirate bond, a brother's attempt to block it) and conflict over property, but the passage is almost entirely dialogue with no narrated outcome. Mainly speech with an event: borderline.

04.missing: a one-time event; this is Rav Huna's habitual practice of asking litigants for a substitute worker
04.reason: A custom cited as precedent with nothing following from it; R-C5 makes a report of practice that leads nowhere not a story.

05.event: walking on the road with a woman ahead of them
05.turn: Rav urges Rav Yehuda to hurry away; Rav Yehuda cites Rav's own leniency
05.outcome: Rav says the leniency applies only to people like R. Hanina bar Pappi, not to them
05.summary: Rav and Rav Yehuda were travelling when a woman walked ahead of them. Rav told Rav Yehuda to hurry away from Gehenna; Rav Yehuda objected that Rav permitted it for the upright, and Rav answered that he meant men like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, not themselves.
05.missing: an explicit narrated action after the dialogue (that they actually hurried)
05.reason: A real situation (walking, the woman) frames an exchange that is mainly speech, with the implied action of hurrying away; mainly speech but something happens, R-C7 shape 1.

06.missing: any narrated event; only an instruction quoted to resolve a legal question
06.reason: A quoted instruction cited within the legal give-and-take, with no event narrated; speech without an event or conflict is not a story.

07.actor: a brewer, the beer owner, Rava
07.event: the brewer betroths a woman with beer sediment belonging to the owner
07.turn: the owner finds him and says he should have used the better sediment
07.outcome: Rava rules the owner's remark is not consent and the betrothal is invalid
07.summary: A brewer betrothed a woman with sediment from the beer he was making for someone else. The owner found him and asked why he had not used the sharper, better sediment. The brewer came before Rava, who ruled that such a remark counts as consent only for teruma.
07.reason: More than a case brought to a rabbi: the betrothal and the owner's discovery and remark are narrated actions, then Rava rules, like R-C0's cow case. But the change is only the ruling, so it sits at borderline.

08.event: he saw the tongue of the executed Hutzpit the disseminator dragged by a pig
08.turn: he exclaimed that a mouth that produced pearls should lick dust
08.summary: According to one view, Elisha ben Avuya saw the tongue of the executed sage Hutzpit dragged in the dirt by a pig. He cried out that a mouth that had produced pearls was licking dust, and he went out and sinned.
08.reason: A post-biblical sage sees something, reacts, and is changed (apostasy): events, causality and change, even if brief and given as one of two explanations.

09.event: visited Rav Gazza's town where cases arose
09.summary: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin (or bar Zevida) visited a town where cases arose, and he ruled on the fitness of the offspring; Ameimar likewise visited and ruled them fit.
09.missing: any action or change beyond the visit and the ruling
09.reason: A visit, a case and a ruling, transmitted as competing reports of a halakhic precedent; under R-C0's limit and Shabbat 147a, a visit plus a ruling is not a story.

10.missing: any event beyond seeing a place, cited to measure it
10.reason: An eyewitness statement of a site's dimensions used as evidence in a legal objection; nothing happens and nothing follows.

11.actor: Rabbi Yohanan, Rabbi Elazar, Reish Lakish
11.event: Rabbi Elazar refutes Rabbi Yohanan's teaching and he falls silent
11.turn: Yohanan praises Elazar; Reish Lakish reveals it was a baraita from Torat Kohanim
11.outcome: Yohanan learns the whole of Torat Kohanim in three days and masters it in three months
11.summary: Rabbi Yohanan expounded a law about notar; Rabbi Elazar refuted him from a baraita and Yohanan was silent. After Elazar left, Yohanan praised him as expounding like Moses, but Reish Lakish said it was a baraita from Torat Kohanim. Yohanan went out, learned the whole work in three days and understood it in three months.
11.reason: Beyond the scholarly exchange there is a defeat, a revelation and a narrated action with change at the end (Yohanan studies the Sifra), so it has events, causality and change.

12.event: a yevama came to perform halitza
12.outcome: Rabbi Tarfon told them all to respond 'he who had his shoe removed'
12.summary: Rabbi Yehuda recalls sitting before Rabbi Tarfon when a yevama came for halitza, and Tarfon instructed all present to call out the formula.
12.missing: any further action or change beyond the instruction
12.reason: A setting plus an instruction, cited as a source for a law; the coming of the yevama only frames the instruction, so under R-C0's limit and the Shabbat 147a ruling it is not a story.

13.event: he conducted halitza with a slipper, alone, at night
13.outcome: Shmuel disparaged him for following individual opinions
13.summary: Rabba bar Hiyya of Ctesiphon performed a halitza with a felt slipper, as a single judge, at night, and Shmuel remarked sarcastically on his following lone opinions.
13.missing: any consequence or change following the act
13.reason: A report of what someone did, cited for its halakhic content, followed only by a critical remark; a rebuke is ordinary discourse, and one act followed by comment is not a story under R-C5 and R-C0's 2026-10-25 line.

14.actor: Mar Yehuda and Rav Huna bar Yehuda
14.event: Mar Yehuda visits and sees people carrying among unrowed trees
14.outcome: he asks, and Rav Huna answers that he follows Rav Nahman
14.summary: Mar Yehuda visited Rav Huna bar Yehuda's house and saw people carrying among trees not planted in rows. He asked whether Rav Huna rejected Avimi's view, and Rav Huna said he followed Rav Nahman.
14.missing: any event beyond the visit framing a question and answer
14.reason: A setting plus a question and answer on a halakhic point, the shape Jeff ruled not a story at Shabbat 147a.

15.missing: a one-time event; only Shmuel's habitual passing through the gates without comment
15.reason: Shmuel's routine practice cited as evidence in answer to a question; a habit leading nowhere is not a story.

16.missing: a narrated incident; only a general historical claim used as an argument in a baraita
16.reason: The Sages' reply cites a general fact (many were recircumcised in bar Kokhba's day and had children) as an argument; it is part of legal debate, not a narrated event.

17.missing: a one-time event; only a household practice and a ruling about it
17.reason: A habitual practice in Rabbi Pedat's house and his ruling that the beam is a utensil; a custom cited as precedent with nothing following.

18.missing: the incident itself; only that a case occurred and halitza was required
18.reason: An unnarrated incident cited only for its ruling; nothing beyond the ruling is told, so it is not a story.

19.actor: a man suspected with his mother-in-law; Rav Sheshet
19.event: the man passed by his father-in-law's door
19.summary: A man passed by the entrance of his father-in-law's house, and Rav Sheshet had him flogged, because he was suspected regarding his mother-in-law.
19.missing: detail of the incident; it is cited briefly as an objection
19.reason: Something happens and a rabbi responds with an act (lashing), more than a bare ruling, but the incident is only sketched as evidence within the legal discussion; between borderline and not, borderline.

20.actor: Rav Kahana; Mar bar Rav Ashi
20.event: Rav Kahana took a cloth for a firstborn's redemption, valuing it at five sela; Mar bar Rav Ashi bought a cloth worth ten for thirteen
20.summary: Rav Kahana, a priest, accepted a cloth at a pidyon haben and said that to him it was worth five sela. Separately, Mar bar Rav Ashi paid thirteen for a cloth worth ten.
20.missing: any consequence or change; both are cited as precedents
20.reason: Two reports of what someone did, cited as evidence within the legal discussion, with no one responding and nothing following; R-C5.
